turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Peak flow before you go in, best of three was two hundred and eighty litres. He reckons his normal is about four hundred and fifty, but he wasn't sure. Pulse was a hundred and eight, oxygen sat ninety-six percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's helpful. Two-eighty, pulse one-oh-eight, sats ninety-six. Come in, both of you.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Hi. Um, sorry, I'm pretty wound up. I've been wheezing since this cold and I keep grabbing the wrong puffer.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll sort the puffers. Tell me about the cold first.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Sniffles started, I want to say ten days ago? Last Monday-ish. Then the wheeze came on.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was a fortnight, doctor. He was off his food and crook the weekend before last, I was there.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Mum, no. That weekend was a sore throat for like one day and then I was fine. The cold is about ten days. And I'm eating.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll put the illness somewhere between ten days and two weeks, and you two don't quite agree. The wheeze, when did that bit start?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Three or four days into the cold. Worse at night, chest goes tight, and I wake up.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's coughing the whole night. And he is hardly eating, whatever he says. Breakfast untouched three mornings.
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): The cough, yes, mostly at night, that's fair. I'm not hardly eating. I skip breakfast because my chest feels gross in the morning, lunch and dinner are normal.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): So night cough, wheeze, morning chest discomfort, we'll say. Appetite you and your mum see differently, I'll note that as unclear. Any fever?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't think I had a proper fever. Felt hot one night, didn't have a thermometer.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or blood when you cough?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain. No blood. Just the whistle when I breathe out. Is that dangerous, should I be in hospital?
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not from what I'm hearing so far, but I'll listen in a minute. Which inhalers are at home?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Blue and brown, and I mix them up every time. Blue one's the one I've been smashing. Maybe five, six times a day.
[SEG0018] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The brown one is the preventer. He hasn't touched it. Still full, in the side pocket of his bag.
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): I did use it. Yesterday morning, two puffs. Or was it the day before? I thought the brown one was for when you're actually wheezy.

[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Blue reliever, maybe five or six times a day. Brown preventer, you think two puffs once, your mum thinks the counter hasn't moved. Do you know the names and the strength?

[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Blue is salbutamol. I think it's a hundred micrograms a puff, might be two hundred, the label's rubbed off. Brown is budesonide, the sticker says two puffs twice a day, and I know I haven't been doing that.

[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And before you ask, his father takes metformin for his diabetes. That's not Liam's. I only mention it because I panic about things running in the family. I had asthma as a kid myself.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Mum, the metformin thing is not about me. Can the blue one hurt me if I use it that much? And will I get addicted?

[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Salbutamol isn't addictive. Using it five or six times a day means the airways aren't settled, which is why we're here. Your dad's metformin stays his. You were diagnosed with asthma...
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, when I was about seventeen, so five-ish years. I'm twenty-two now. It was quiet until this cold. Do steroids make your face puffy? My friend said they do.

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): A short course doesn't usually do that. I'm thinking this is a flare of your asthma after the virus, not a brand new diagnosis, though I can't prove the virus from here. Let me listen.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's wheeze both sides, a bit louder on the right. No crackles. You're speaking in full sentences, which is reassuring.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): So I'm not dying? What about footy on Saturday, it's a social game, I really don't want to miss it.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): No footy this weekend. If you're still this wheezy I'd rather you rest. We'll add a steroid tablet, prednisolone, fifty milligrams once a day for five days, with food in the morning.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Fifty? That's a lot, isn't it? Do I take it with the brown puffer or instead? And what if I vomit it up, do I take another?

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): With the brown one, not instead. If you vomit within half an hour, yes, repeat that dose once. Keep the blue one for symptoms, two puffs at a time, but I don't want you needing it all day.
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should he start the budesonide properly, two puffs twice a day, from today?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. Two puffs, twice a day, every day, even when he feels better. Shake it, and rinse his mouth after.

[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Rinse, okay. What if I forget the night one? The chemist was out of spacers last week, does that matter? Also my sister takes biotin gummies for her hair, she said they help energy, should I get some?

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Biotin is your sister's, skip it, it won't touch the wheeze. A spacer helps, but don't delay the steroid waiting on one. If you miss a night dose, take the morning one as normal, don't double up.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright. Um, will I need an x-ray? My uncle had pneumonia and I'm scared that's what this is.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't think so today. Chest is wheeze without crackles, and the sats are alright. If it hasn't settled in a week we might organise a chest x-ray.
[SEG0038] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His uncle's pneumonia was years ago, different person. Liam, stop spiralling.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm not spiralling, I'm asking. What numbers should worry me? The two hundred and eighty sounds bad.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Two-eighty is lower than the four-fifty you guessed, so yes it's down, but that usual figure was a guess. Come back and see me in five days, sooner if you can't speak a sentence, the blue inhaler isn't helping, or your lips look blue.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Five days. Do I come here or the hospital? And can Mum book it, I start work at eight.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Here, with me, in five days. Your mum can book it at the desk on the way out. Hospital only if those warning signs happen.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): What about driving? And showers, steam makes me cough sometimes. Is that a thing?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short drives are fine if you feel steady. Steam can irritate a twitchy airway, so cooler showers for a few days. That's common, not a new problem.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll keep an ear on the night cough. He shares the house with me and his sister, so I'll hear it.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Please don't sit outside my door, Mum. Doctor, if the prednisolone upsets my stomach, do I stop?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it for mild nausea, take it with food. Ring us if you get severe tummy pain or vomiting you can't keep down. I'll write the five-day course now.
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the peak flow on the slip, two hundred and eighty, so the file has it. Want me to book that five-day review?
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes please, five days, with me. And the prednisolone script is going to the chemist electronically.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Wait, one more. If I feel better on day three, do I finish the tablets? I hate taking things I don't need.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Finish all five days even if you feel better on day three. Brown puffer continues after that. We'll check the peak flow again when you're back.

spec.situation: Teenager or adult wheezy after a cold; confuses blue and brown inhaler; uses the reliever 'maybe five, six times a day'; peak flow numbers read by the nurse. Doctor adds a steroid course.
features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

bad.reason: Cough mostly at night is supported; steam aggravation was discussed by doctor, not stated as established symptom.
